title: The oldest trick
summary_es: Un ensayo sobre la persuasión: las tres vías de Aristóteles, por qué el carácter y la emoción pesan más que la lógica y qué podemos hacer al respecto.
prediction_prompt: Think of the last advertisement that convinced you. Was it an argument that persuaded you, or something else?

sentences.text: Rarely do we notice persuasion while it is happening.
We tend to imagine it as something done to other people, the gullible and the uninformed, by advertisers and politicians.
We ourselves merely weigh the evidence and reach conclusions.
This flattering picture is, of course, exactly what a skilled persuader would want us to believe.
The systematic study of how minds are changed is at least twenty-four centuries old.
Aristotle, lecturing in Athens, divided the means of persuasion into three.
A speaker may appeal to reason, offering arguments and proof.
He may appeal to emotion, stirring anger, fear or pity in his audience.
Or he may rely on character: the impression that he is the kind of person who can be trusted.
The Greek terms for these three, logos, pathos and ethos, have survived in textbooks ever since, which is itself a tribute to how little the essentials have changed.
What strikes a modern reader is the order of importance Aristotle assigned to them.
We like to think that reason comes first.
He suspected otherwise.
Character, he observed, is very nearly the most powerful of the three, for we believe good people more readily than others, and we do so most of all on questions where certainty is impossible.
Not until the twentieth century did psychologists confirm the point experimentally: the same statement is judged more convincing when attributed to a source the listener already respects.
In one famous study, American students were shown an article about medicine.
Half were told that it came from a respected scientific journal, the rest that it came from a popular magazine.
The text was identical; the degree of belief was not.
Consider how this works in an ordinary advertisement.
A toothpaste is recommended by a figure in a white coat.
No argument is offered; none is needed.
The coat does the work that evidence would otherwise have to do.
Nor is the technique confined to commerce.
A politician who rolls up his sleeves before speaking, or who mentions, in passing, the town where he grew up, is not giving reasons to vote for him.
He is constructing a self.
Emotion operates differently but no less efficiently.
Feelings narrow attention.
A frightened audience wants a solution, and it is seldom in the mood to compare alternatives.
This is why so many appeals follow the same pattern in two steps: first the threat, vividly described, and then, with a certain generosity, the remedy.
Sellers of insurance and of alarm systems have understood this for generations, as have the authors of political speeches.
Only by recognising the pattern can a listener begin to separate the two and ask whether the remedy actually answers the threat.
None of this means that reason is powerless.
Arguments do change minds, particularly over time and particularly when they are repeated by people we like.
But logic rarely travels alone.
Even the driest scientific paper persuades partly through its conventions: the cautious phrasing, the list of references, the institutions named beneath the authors.
These are signals of character dressed as formalities.
A reader who would never trust a stranger in the street will trust the same stranger in a footnote.
It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that rhetoric is merely a collection of tricks to be exposed.
Aristotle certainly did not think so.
For him, the art of persuasion was morally neutral, like the art of medicine, which can cure or poison according to the intentions of whoever practises it.
A just cause argued badly will lose to an unjust one argued well; hence the honest have, if anything, a greater duty to master the craft than the dishonest.
The implication for the rest of us is less comfortable than the flattering picture with which we began.
We cannot opt out of being persuaded, any more than we can opt out of hearing.
What we can do is become slower: to notice who is speaking before we attend to what is said, and to notice what we are feeling before we decide what we think.
It sounds like very little, and in a sense it is.
Under no circumstances will this make us immune.
It may, however, make us slightly more expensive to convince, and that, in a crowded marketplace of voices, is no small thing.

language_focus.title_es: Inversión tras un elemento negativo o restrictivo
language_focus.explanation_es: *Rarely do we notice…*, *Not until the twentieth century did psychologists confirm…*, *Only by recognising the pattern can a listener…*, *Under no circumstances will this…*: cuando la frase empieza así, el auxiliar va delante del sujeto, como en una pregunta. Da énfasis y es propio del registro formal.
*Nor is the technique confined to commerce*: *nor* añade una segunda negación y también obliga a invertir.

tasks.prompt: What is the central argument of the essay?

options.text: Persuasion works mainly through logic and careful, patient reasoning with facts
Persuasion leans on character and emotion, and noticing this helps
Rhetoric is a dishonest art that should be banned
Aristotle's ideas are now out of date

tasks.rationale_es: El carácter y la emoción pesan más de lo que creemos; darse cuenta nos hace algo más difíciles de convencer.

tasks.prompt: Match paragraphs 2, 4, 5 and 7 with the best heading. There is one extra heading.
tasks.rationale_es: El párrafo 2 presenta las tres vías; el 4, el ejemplo de la bata blanca; el 5, el patrón amenaza-remedio; el 7, la retórica como arte neutral.

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer call the picture in paragraph 1 "flattering"?

options.text: Because it presents us as more rational than we are
Because advertisers constantly praise their loyal customers
Because Aristotle admired his audience
Because it is accurate

tasks.rationale_es: Nos gusta creer que a nosotros no nos persuaden: eso es justo lo que querría un buen persuasor.

tasks.prompt: Which did Aristotle consider close to the most powerful means of persuasion?

options.text: Reason
Emotion
Character
Repetition

tasks.rationale_es: *Character… is very nearly the most powerful of the three*.

tasks.prompt: What did experiments in the twentieth century show?

options.text: Emotional messages are forgotten quickly
Logical arguments always win in the end
People trust a statement less each time it is repeated to them
Who says something affects how convincing it seems

tasks.rationale_es: La misma frase convence más si se atribuye a una fuente que el oyente ya respeta.

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 4, "He is constructing a self" means the politician is…

options.text: building an image of who he is
writing his autobiography
telling lies about his opponents in the campaign
explaining his policies

tasks.rationale_es: No da razones: fabrica una imagen de sí mismo.

tasks.prompt: According to the writer, the figure in the white coat presents scientific evidence.
tasks.rationale_es: *No argument is offered; none is needed*: la bata hace el trabajo de las pruebas.

options.text: reason and emotion
the threat and the remedy
the speaker and the audience
fear and anger

tasks.rationale_es: Los dos pasos del patrón: la amenaza y el remedio.

tasks.prompt: What does the writer suggest about scientific papers?

options.text: They are entirely free of any kind of persuasion
They are deliberately dishonest
Their formal features also signal trustworthiness
Nobody reads their references

tasks.rationale_es: Las convenciones (cautela, referencias, instituciones) transmiten credibilidad.
La consideraba moralmente neutral, como la medicina.

tasks.prompt: Why do honest people have "a greater duty to master the craft"?

options.text: Because they are naturally poor speakers in public
Since being right is not enough to win people over
Because the dishonest never study rhetoric
Because Aristotle required it of his students

tasks.rationale_es: Una causa justa mal defendida pierde ante una injusta bien defendida.

tasks.prompt: What does the writer ultimately recommend?

options.text: Refusing to listen to advertisements
Trusting only scientists
Studying ancient Greek
Watching the speaker and our own feelings

tasks.rationale_es: Ir más despacio: fijarse en quién habla y en qué sentimos antes de decidir qué pensamos.

tasks.prompt: Aristotle wrote his work on rhetoric late in his life.
tasks.rationale_es: Se dice que enseñaba en Atenas, no en qué momento de su vida escribió sobre retórica.
